newsitem.title: CHINA: China mulls new curbs on foreign law firms.
newsitem.headline: China mulls new curbs on foreign law firms.

text.p: China is planning new curbs on foreign law firms that would substantially limit their business and dramatically raise operating costs, foreign lawyers and businessmen said on Friday.
They said they were "extremely concerned" over the measures, which could hinder foreign investment and appeared to be aimed at protecting domestic firms from competition.
The curbs, which have been shown to foreign firms in draft form, would bar foreign law firms from hiring Chinese nationals as lawyers or legal assistants.

They would also require the chief representative of a foreign law firm to hold a passport from the company's home country and put minimum requirements on the experience of those lawyers working in China.

Foreign businessmen said the new rules, which were presented by the Ministry of Justice as an interpretation of regulations dating back to 1992, appeared to be an effort by local law firms to head off competition from foreigners.
"The intent appears to be to stop foreign law firms from advising foreign clients on Chinese law," said a Western consultant who has been following the issue closely.
"The rules would also substantially raise the cost for lawyers doing business in China and could force some of them to close up shop," he said.
An official at the Ministry of Justice said no new regulations were being implemented or were being studied.
Asked whether interpretations of existing legislation were planned, he said: "I am unaware of that."
Western businessmen met on Wednesday night to review reports of the planned changes and try to present their views to Chinese authorities before the rules went into effect.
They said the rules would be announced in the next week or two and could take effect as early as January.
"The American business community is very concerned," said James McGregor, chairman of the American Chamber of Commerce in Beijing.
"If this is implemented it would be a real step backward for foreign investment," he said.
Lawyers said the regulations would affect their ability to analyse domestic legal issues on behalf of foreign clients.
While they cannot practise law in China and are supposed to advise on international legal matters, they often offer analysis on China's legal environment to foreign investors.
Many foreign law firms employ Chinese nationals who have been trained overseas to do this.
The impact would be hardest on smaller law firms, many of them European, which have hired Americans or a Chinese national as a represenative.
Regulations that also require more experienced lawyers to work in China would also push up costs and drive some of the smaller firms out of the market.
Foreign lawyers said they saw this as yet more evidence that China was worried about foreign competition in a wide range of industries.
The local media has been full of reports of the devastating effect of foreign products on domestic manufacturers, particularly state enterprises.

Foreign businessmen said this was not an encouraging sign for those hoping that China would remove some of its existing barriers to foreign companies as it seeks to join the World Trade Organisation, the global trade body.
A Chinese lawyer who asked not to be identified said there were now 72 foreign law firms operating in China and the competition was growing.
He added that the new restrictions would help local law firms -- such as his own -- though this form of protection was not needed for all domestic lawyers.
"We have lots of work already," he said. "We don't need this kind of help."
